title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory comparison of (A) a generation‑only pipeline and (C) a generate→validate→simulate→rollback (guarded) pipeline for LLM‑assisted NetOps configuration tasks. Under a frozen design (preregistration id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) we ran gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing, ACL, NAT). A deterministic simulator adjudicated an actionable‑misconfiguration binary per task (actionable misconfiguration = 1; non‑actionable/safe = 0). Results: baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) [0.00,0.00]; McNemar exact p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is not evaluable because the baseline actionable rate was zero (ceiling effect). We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs, scoring artifacts, and analysis traces (artifact hashes recorded in the execution manifest). We discuss construct and external validity, limitations, and directions for more challenging task sets, multi‑model evaluation, and richer validators.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and limited self‑healing. However, operational risk arises when fluent model outputs are enacted without effective pre‑enactment assurance [VeriFlow 2012; Mondal et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2025]. Prior work advocates generate→validate→repair architectures, but evidence tying LLM generation to deterministic enactment outcomes under a preregistered plan is sparse. We preregistered a paired confirmatory study (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) that asks: does a generate→validate→simulate→rollback (guarded) pipeline (C) reduce the actionable‑misconfiguration rate by ≥30% relative to a generation‑only baseline (A) on a representative vendor‑neutral task set? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifacted, paired execution using gpt‑5‑mini; (2) deterministic simulator adjudication of enactability with traceable scoring artifacts; (3) transparent reporting of a ceiling effect and concrete recommendations for future harder benchmarks.
sections.related_work: We situate the work relative to three streams: (i) network verification and update checking (VeriFlow and later verifiers) that operationalize fast invariants checks on control/data planes [Khurshid et al., VeriFlow 2012]; (ii) LLM‑for‑NetOps generation with constraint/validator augmentation (e.g., Verified Prompt Programming, MeshAgent) that combine generation with local verification or constraint encoding; (iii) Ops/AIOps benchmark efforts (OpsEval family, LogEval) that emphasize task realism. Distinctive here is the preregistered, paired execution linking generation to deterministic enactment outcomes with full artifact hashes and a frozen analysis plan.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The full experimental plan (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) froze task selection, seeds, metrics, stopping/retry rules, and analysis before execution. Design: paired confirmatory comparison (baseline A vs guarded C) on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing ≈64, ACL ≈64, NAT/other ≈32). Model and prompting: single hosted model gpt‑5‑mini; one shared initial generation call per task (pre‑registered). Guarded pipeline: generation → constraint/validator → deterministic simulator enactment → automatic rollback scoring. Baseline: generation only; simulator scored the generated configuration but no pre‑enactment blocking. Primary outcome and terminology (clarified per reviewer): the per‑task binary outcome is 'actionable misconfiguration' defined as 1 when the deterministic simulator detects a safety violation that would make the configuration unsafe to enact; 0 denotes non‑actionable/safe. Primary estimand: paired difference in actionable proportion A − C. Analysis: paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) for CI; McNemar exact test for paired binary outcomes. Reproducibility: all prompts, seeds, canonicalizers, simulator, raw model outputs, scoring JSONs, and analysis scripts archived; artifact paths and SHA‑256 hashes are recorded in the execution manifest and the run artifacts (see Disclosure).
sections.results: Execution completed per the preregistered plan (execution manifest and artifact hashes archived). Numerical facts (artifact‑backed): N=160 paired tasks; baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160. Contingency table: n11 (non‑actionable in both) = 160; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. Paired difference (A−C) = 0.00. Bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729): [0.00,0.00]. McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00. Operational note: across the confirmatory set the guarded validator did not block any generated configuration that the simulator later labelled actionable (blocked count = 0 on the confirmatory tasks). All per‑task scoring JSONs, provider call logs, and analysis artifacts are archived (see Disclosure for hashes).
sections.discussion: Interpretation and construct validity: the preregistered effect (≥30% relative reduction) is undefined when baseline=0 (ceiling effect). The degenerate result is an empirical fact in the archived artifacts, not evidence that the guarded pipeline is unnecessary in general. Three artifact‑backed explanations (non‑exclusive): (1) Task calibration: the confirmatory task set produced generated outputs that the chosen simulator predicate judged non‑actionable (task difficulty was too low under the predicate). (2) Predicate scope: the deterministic simulator encodes a specific safety predicate; it may miss other real‑world hazards (construct validity). (3) Model and prompt scope: results apply to gpt‑5‑mini under the supplied prompts and call budget only (single‑model external validity threat). Operational implication: guarded pipelines can reduce enactable faults only when baseline generation produces enactable faults detectable by the chosen validator. Recommendations: (i) future confirmatory runs should use adversarial/harder task sets calibrated to yield a nonzero baseline actionable rate; (ii) evaluate multiple models and prompt variants; (iii) expand scoring predicates and/or include human adjudication for broader construct coverage. Reproducibility: all raw outputs, scoring JSONs, and analysis scripts are provided in the archived artifacts (execution/raw_results.jsonl and per‑task scoring JSONs; hashes below).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation of a generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline versus generation‑only for LLM‑assisted NetOps using gpt‑5‑mini on 160 confirmatory tasks. Observed outcome: both conditions produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the deterministic simulator (paired difference 0.00, 95% CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p=1.00). Because baseline=0, the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target is not evaluable (ceiling effect). The result highlights the critical importance of task calibration, multi‑model scope, and richer scoring predicates when assessing operational benefits of guarded pipelines. We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs, scoring artifacts, and analysis traces so future work can re‑score, extend, or run harder confirmatory sets against the same archived materials.

disclosure_statement:
Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track).

Models, adapter, and orchestration: primary generative model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Orchestration and execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family under the frozen preregistered plan c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1. The exact initial master prompt bundle (Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run) and the autonomy boundary are recorded in the preregistration and manifest. Topic constraints: the Research Director selected the broad family “Generative AI and Large Language Models for NetOps” and constrained the scope to operational reliability, validation, and enactability; those constraints are recorded in the preregistration.

Pre‑lock development and autonomy boundary: collaborative pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred and were explicitly excluded from final empirical evidence as required by the track. After the autonomy lock, literature search, research‑gap selection, preregistration, prompt generation, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, autonomous peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously. No human manually edited technical manuscript content, numerical results, figures, captions, references, or the Disclosure Statement after the autonomy lock.

Preregistration and frozen design: the full experimental plan is preregistered as c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 and was frozen before execution (the preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the archived run: 63ddaeb125915145884c55ac5c1d1409a31c3204e21206f2945317d8e61714dc). Key preregistered elements included: task selection rules, augmentation seeds, model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), maximum model calls (320), paired confirmatory design (N=160 tasks), primary metric (actionable misconfiguration binary), analysis plan (paired bootstrap 10k, McNemar exact), retry policy, and stopping rules. Any deviations would be logged; none affecting confirmatory outcomes occurred.

Execution artifacts and access: all experiment artifacts (preregistration, raw model outputs, provider call logs, canonicalized configurations, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator, analysis scripts, and the execution manifest) are archived in the run artifact bundle. The primary raw results file recorded in the execution manifest is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044). The preregistration SHA‑256 is 63ddaeb125915145884c55ac5c1d1409a31c3204e21206f2945317d8e61714dc. The execution manifest contains explicit per‑artifact paths and SHA‑256 hashes (for example, per‑task scoring JSONs and provider call logs); those manifest entries are the canonical record for integrity‑verified replication and re‑scoring. Where public hosting is not provided in this submission package, interested reviewers and researchers may verify integrity against the listed SHA‑256 values in the execution manifest. No additional external URLs or repository locations are invented or claimed in this statement.

Model calls and retries: the preregistered maximum model calls was 320; actual model calls used = 160 (one shared initial generation per task). Provider call logs, per‑call caching, and the call cache artifacts are archived (see execution manifest). Retries were pre‑registered (up to two) for transient provider failures; no persistent failures affected confirmatory outcomes.

Human role and limitations: the human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; post‑lock scientific execution and manuscript drafting were autonomous. Precise provider endpoint identifiers and internal provider operational logs are not published here for confidentiality; everything required to reproduce the analysis given the same hosted model API (prompts, seeds, canonicalizers, simulator, raw outputs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256) is archived and referenced in the execution manifest. The manifest and artifact SHA‑256 hashes are authoritative for verification of the run.
limitations: Confirmatory task set produced a ceiling effect (baseline generation judged non‑actionable by the simulator), preventing evaluation of the preregistered relative‑reduction target (≥30%).
Single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize to other foundation models or prompt variants without additional runs.
Deterministic simulator safety predicate is an abstraction and may not capture all real‑world operational failure modes (construct validity).
Public/synthetic vendor‑neutral tasks were used; no live device enactment or production telemetry was executed (external validity).
Potential residual contamination risk from overlap between public corpus and model training data was mitigated per preregistered hashing and similarity checks, but cannot be fully excluded.
